Eggs of the Moss froglet (Crinia nimbus) contain a substantial initial energy reserve; the total energy content measured for each fertilised ovum was 249 J . This yolk-laden egg provides the sole nutritional source for the developing embryo until the onset of exogenous feeding. At the moment of hatching, when the chorion ruptures and the aquatic larva emerges, the residual energy has been drawn down considerably. Laboratory studies have recorded that at the hatching event the energy content is 35 J plus an additional 167 J, which is to say 202 J  in total at eclosion. This dramatic consumption of the yolk energy over the course of embryogenesis highlights the high metabolic demands of early development in this cool-adapted species. The endotrophic, pre-feeding tadpole then continues to rely on its remaining yolk reserves, and by the time the mouth opens and first feeding begins, the energy content has been further reduced. Measurements indicate that the energy at the transition to first exogenous feeding is 123 J plus 49 J, totalling 172 J  at birth, representing a substantial depletion of the original egg capital. This energetic trajectory from egg through hatching to the onset of independent feeding is relatively steep compared to some other Australian myobatrachids.

The size of Crinia nimbus individuals undergoes a marked transformation as they progress through the larval and post-metamorphic stages. Hatchlings that emerge following the gel dissolution of the jelly capsule are relatively diminutive, measuring a total length of 0.5 cm  from snout to tail tip. This initial size reflects the brief period of intra-egg development when the embryo is still largely dependent on yolk. As the yolk-sac larva develops and begins to feed exogenously, it grows to a total length of 0.72 cm [Lb = 0.72 cm] at birth, marking the stage when the larval amphibian is fully independent of its yolk reserves. Over the subsequent weeks of active feeding as an herbivorous, filter-feeding tadpole, growth accelerates considerably. Upon completing the larval-juvenile transition and undergoing the metamorphic climax, the froglet continues to increase in size until it reaches its ultimate total length of 2.7 cm [Li = 2.7 cm] as a reproductively active adult. This asymptotic length is modest even by the standards of myobatrachid frogs and is likely a consequence of the species' short activity season.

Body mass measurements taken from captive-reared individuals provide a detailed picture of growth and development. At hatching, the yolk-dependent tadpole had a wet weight of 0.023 grams , while the corresponding dry weight was 0.0086 grams . By the time the larval amphibian had completed the yolk-sac resorption and commenced first feeding, the wet weight had increased to 0.0318 grams [Wwb = 0.0318 grams] overall at birth, and the dry weight at this same stage was 0.0079 grams . The modest increase in wet mass coupled with a slight decline in dry mass between hatching and birth is expected, as the tadpole is transitioning from a yolk-dependent lecithotrophic larva to a feeding, exotrophic tadpole, during which the body composition shifts from dense yolk to more hydrated tissues. Eventually, adults attain an ultimate wet weight of 1.67 grams [Wwi = 1.67 grams], a value that is consistent with the small body size evident from the ultimate total length.

Developmental timing in Crinia nimbus is highly sensitive to ambient thermal conditions, as is typical for temperate anurans. When incubated at 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the period from fertilisation to the moment of eclosion lasted 75 days , at which the shell breaks and the embryo emerges, whereas at the same temperature the transition to the birth stage, defined as the completion of yolk absorption and commencement of first feeding, required 277 days [ab = 277 days]. At a warmer incubation temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], developmental rates accelerated appreciably: age at hatch was recorded at 44 days , and the time to birth was just 149 days [ab = 149 days]. The most extreme thermal condition tested was 5 °C [T = 5 °C], at which point development slowed and hatching did not occur until 169 days  after fertilisation. These results demonstrate that the temperature during embryonic and larval development has a profound effect on the duration of the yolk-dependent and exotrophic phases. The extended ab at low temperatures likely reflects a reduction in metabolic and biosynthetic rates, which prolongs the period required to mobilise yolk reserves and complete organogenesis.

Longevity and reproductive scheduling in the Moss froglet are similarly influenced by temperature and body size. At 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the maximum recorded longevity for individuals maintained under semi-natural laboratory conditions is 2920 days [am = 2920 days], which corresponds to approximately eight years. This extended lifespan is considerable for a frog of such small body size, and it implies a relatively slow pace of ageing, possibly linked to the cool thermal environment that depresses metabolic rate. First reproduction in this species, defined as the first amplexus and successful egg deposition, occurs at 912 days after the time of birth [tR = 912 days after the time of birth] when individuals are maintained at 14 °C [T = 14 °C]. This protracted delay before the first breeding event is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritises growth and the attainment of a sufficient body size before investing in reproduction. The maximum reproductive rate, measured under the same thermal conditions of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], is approximately 16 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 16 eggs per year], a figure that is likely constrained by the limited number of clutches a female can produce within the short activity season. This combination of a long life, delayed maturation, and modest annual fecundity situates Crinia nimbus at the slow end of the fast-slow continuum among Australian myobatrachids.
